Problem 593. Applying a rule with an exception: Arun
Rules often have conditions and exceptions. Logical reading prevents us from applying a general rule when an overriding exception is active.

Arun is 14 years old. A library rule says: a child may enter the archive room if age ≥ 13 AND an adult permit is present. Exception: during an evacuation drill, nobody may enter. Permit present: yes. Evacuation drill: no.
Check exceptions first if they override the general rule. Otherwise every condition joined by AND must be true.
May Arun enter the archive room under these facts? Show which conditions succeed or fail.
1. Age test: 14≥13 is True. 2. Permit test is True. 3. Because the general rule uses AND, both tests must pass. 4. Therefore entry is allowed.
The order of reasoning matters when exceptions override ordinary rules.
Boolean rule with priority: exception predicate first, then conjunction of eligibility conditions.

C2. Rights as limits on decisions
Problem 596. Majority rule and a protected right: case 1
Democratic procedures use voting, but constitutional systems can place some rights beyond ordinary majority power.

A council of 20 members votes 15 to 5 for a proposal that would forbid one named group from the right to speak at a peaceful meeting. The classroom constitution states: (1) ordinary proposals pass by simple majority; (2) an ordinary majority may not remove the listed equal rights from a group.
A decision must satisfy both the voting procedure and the higher rights constraint. Passing a vote is not sufficient if the content violates a protected right.
Did the proposal receive a majority? May it take effect under the stated constitution?

1. Vote check: 15>5, so the proposal has a simple majority. 2. Content check: the proposal removes a protected equal right (speak at a peaceful meeting) from a group. 3. The higher rights rule therefore blocks the proposal even though the vote passed.
